target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would give everyone the time and flexibility to vote by removing scheduling barriers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to provide paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar jobs would still have to work or lose income; therefore the holiday would not reliably remove voting barriers for the people most constrained by work schedules.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday would not meaningfully reduce scheduling barriers because it does not guarantee paid leave for every private worker.
objection: Even without guaranteed paid leave, a national holiday still meaningfully reduces barriers because it changes the baseline for schools, government offices, and everyday obligations, giving many people more predictable, coordinated time to vote and helping them rearrange responsibilities around a public off-day.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday substantially alters the baseline hours most Americans are free to vote.
objection: A holiday does not oblige private employers to stop operating or release workers with paid leave, so for many low-income workers in essential customer-facing jobs the binding constraint remains work schedule and lack of protected time off, not the closure of schools or government offices.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday will not meaningfully reduce scheduling barriers because private employers may still operate.
objection: The barrier to voting is not only employer-provided paid leave; a holiday also eases everyday obligations such as childcare and errands, changes the day's baseline for many households, and creates a coordinated public off-day that helps even some low-income workers better rearrange their time.

target: AG1's broader argument that a national holiday is an effective turnout policy.
objection: Research indicates that simply designating Election Day a holiday generally does not produce strong turnout gains compared with reforms that directly remove voting obstacles, so the policy is a poor tradeoff if the goal is to increase voting.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is not an effective turnout reform and mainly symbolic.
objection: A national holiday directly tackles the real time-conflict problem created by school and work obligations by creating a coordinated public off-day, making voting easier to plan around and reducing the barrier that suppresses turnout for millions.

target: AG1's premise that a holiday directly tackles the time-conflict problem even without guaranteed paid leave.
objection: That argument assumes the holiday will actually give most schedule-constrained voters a usable time window, but many workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and other essential jobs will still be scheduled to work, so the holiday does not remove their time constraint.

target: AG2's broader claim that a holiday does not meaningfully address the time-based obstacle to voting.
objection: Election Day as a holiday directly reduces the real scheduling conflict created by school and work obligations by making voting part of a coordinated public off-day, so it is not merely symbolic but a practical access improvement.

target: AG1's assumption that a national holiday will reliably create a coordinated public off-day that eases school/work conflicts.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or give paid time off, so many workers—especially in essential and low-wage jobs—will still have the same work obligations, meaning the holiday will not reliably create the flexible time to vote that the pro-holiday argument assumes.
